pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; interpret a multiplication equation as a COMPARISON (35 = 5×7 means 35 is 5 times as many as 7), and translate verbal multiplicative-comparison statements into equations.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4–Y5 scaling problems ('n times as tall/heavy/many') and multiplicative reasoning underpinning ratio.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.1 — 'interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g. 35 = 5×7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.'
• Operational details — this is a NEW meaning of multiplication beyond equal groups: a relationship between two quantities where one is 'n times' the other. The load-bearing distinction is multiplicative ('5 times as many') vs additive ('5 more') — children habitually confuse them. Teach with the comparison bar model: a short bar (the referent) and a bar n times as long (the compared quantity); the scale factor is the multiplier. Note 35=5×7 supports TWO comparisons (35 is 5 times 7 AND 7 times 5). This is the conceptual seed of ratio, rate and proportion.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): translate '4 times as many' to ×4 and draw the two bars. Tier B (age 9–10): write an equation for a verbal multiplicative-comparison statement. Tier C (age 10): distinguish multiplicative from additive comparison and explain both comparisons a single equation encodes.
bestPractices: Use the comparison bar model — referent bar vs a bar n times as long — so 'times as many' is seen as a scaling relationship, not an equal-groups count.
Directly contrast multiplicative ('5 times as many') with additive ('5 more') using the same numbers, since children conflate them.
Show that one equation (35=5×7) encodes two comparisons, building flexibility.
Move both ways — verbal→equation and equation→verbal — to secure the translation.
Frame it as the gateway to ratio/rate so the multiplicative relationship is seen as foundational.
keyRepresentations: Comparison bar model (referent bar and the n-times bar)
Double number line — the scaling relationship between two quantities
Scale-factor arrow (×n) between the two quantities
commonMisconceptions: Confusing multiplicative comparison ('3 times as many') with additive ('3 more').
Treating multiplicative comparison as equal groups and losing the relational meaning.
Getting the direction wrong (which quantity is the referent / which is n times the other).
Not seeing that 35=5×7 expresses both '5 times 7' and '7 times 5'.
Adding when the language says 'times as many' (or vice versa).

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: interpret a multiplication equation as a COMPARISON (35 = 5×7 means 35 is 5 times as many as 7, and also 7 times as many as 5) and translate verbal 'n times as many' statements into equations. The load-bearing distinction is multiplicative ('5 times as many') versus additive ('5 more') — children habitually confuse these. Activities centre on the comparison bar model (a referent bar and a bar n times as long), explicit multiplicative-vs-additive contrast using the same numbers, two-way verbal↔equation translation, and the insight that a single equation encodes two multiplicative comparisons. This is the conceptual seed of ratio, rate and proportion.

activities.title: Scaling bars: times as many vs more than
feedback: If the additive and multiplicative bars come out the same, re-count: 5 copies of 7 (end-to-end) is very different from 7 with 5 added on. Compare the two blue bars directly.
If the equation direction is reversed, name the referent first: red is 'one unit', blue is n of those units, so blue = n × red.
When you re-read the bars, check both statements describe the same picture: if 35 is 5 times 7, then 7 is one of the 5 equal parts of 35.
activities.rationale: Building and comparing bars makes the multiplicative-vs-additive difference concrete using the same numbers, which is exactly the confusion to resolve; re-reading one picture two ways builds relational flexibility. An optional live version (a ×n dial that recolours/rescales the blue bar while the equation updates, with a toggle overlaying an additive 'ghost' bar) can make the contrast dynamic, but stacking physical or drawn copies achieves the same insight.

4.OA.1 requires interpreting a multiplication equation as a comparison and representing verbal multiplicative comparisons as equations.
Y4–Y5 pupils solve scaling ('n times as many') problems, developing the multiplicative reasoning that underpins ratio.
learnerActions: Start with a short referent bar labelled red (e.g. red = 7). Build a second bar, blue, that is 'n times as long' by stacking n copies of the red bar end to end; for ×5 this makes blue = 35.

Alongside the multiplicative bar, build an ADDITIVE comparison bar: red plus a fixed amount (red + 5 = 12). Place the two blue results side by side so '5 times as many' (35) visibly towers over '5 more' (12).
Write the equation that matches the multiplicative bars: blue = n × red (e.g. blue = 5 × red, so blue = 35).

Re-read the SAME pair of bars (7 and 35) two ways: the multiplicative-comparison statement '35 is 5 times as many as 7', and its reciprocal '7 is one-fifth of 35 / 7 is one of the five equal copies that make 35'. State both out loud. (The matching equation 35 = 5 × 7 also carries two multiplicative comparisons — '35 is 5 times as many as 7' and '35 is 7 times as many as 5' — which you will write out in the sort-and-translate activity.)
Take verbal cards such as 'Sarah has 3 times as many stickers as Tom, who has 8' and build the correct bars, then write the equation (3 × 8 = 24).
activities.intendedInsight: 'n times as many' is a scaling relationship — n copies of the referent — not n added on; and the same pair of bars can be read two ways: the multiplicative comparison '35 is 5 times as many as 7' and its reciprocal '7 is one-fifth of 35'.

activities.title: Tower comparison: how many copies fit?
feedback: If the answer is 8 ('4 taller' / 'add 4'): that is the additive reading. Physically stack four whole red towers to see four copies — '4 more' only adds 4 cubes, which is a much shorter tower.

If red and blue get swapped (computing 4 ÷ 16 or treating blue as the unit): name red as the single unit and show blue is 4 of those units (16 ÷ 4 = 4); a double number line with red at 1 and blue at 4 helps.
If 16 is computed but explained only as '4 times 4' with no meaning: ask 'how many red towers would you need to match blue?' to surface the copies-of relationship already implicit in the answer.
activities.rationale: A referent/compared pair with a clean right answer (16, not 8) targets the signature additive error directly; asking for the meaning, not just the number, reveals copies-of versus more-than reasoning.
sourceClaims: Comparison bar models support multiplicative comparison; multiplicative and additive comparison must be explicitly contrasted.
learnerActions: The red tower is 4 cubes tall; the blue tower is 4 TIMES as tall. Build blue by stacking four separate red towers end to end, then count: 4 × 4 = 16 cubes.
Explain in words what '4 times as tall' means: blue is four copies of red's height.
Now build a '4 MORE than red' tower (4 + 4 = 8) beside it and describe how it differs from the '4 times' tower.
Given both towers (red = 4, blue = 16), work out how many times as tall blue is, and say how you know (how many red towers fit into blue).
Try a variant: if red were 5 cubes and blue is 4 times as tall, how tall is blue? (20)
activities.intendedInsight: 'Times as tall' compares by how many COPIES of the referent fit, not by how many more; the multiplier tells you how many copies.

activities.title: Sort and translate: multiplicative or additive?
feedback: A statement that uses 'times as many' but is matched to a '+' equation is the core confusion — reread it as copies: '5 times as many' means 5 copies, so multiply.
When writing the two statements for one equation, swap which factor is the referent: 5×7 reads as both '5 copies of 7' (35 is 5 times 7) and '7 copies of 5' (35 is 7 times 5).
activities.rationale: Checking translation and the multiplicative/additive distinction with targeted contrasting items (×5 versus +5 on the same numbers) verifies whether the relational meaning is secure. A sort/match task can check recognition and translation, but it does not itself elicit the scaling feel, so pair it with the bar-building work above.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.1 requires interpreting a multiplication equation as a comparison and representing verbal multiplicative comparisons as equations.
Comparison bar models support multiplicative comparison; multiplicative and additive comparison must be explicitly contrasted.
learnerActions: Sort word-problem statements into two piles: 'times as many' (multiplicative) and 'more than' (additive). Example multiplicative: 'Sam has 5 times as many as Jo.' Example additive: 'Sam has 5 more than Jo.'
Match each verbal statement to its equation, e.g. 'Sam has 5 times as many' → ×5 (not +5).
Translate both ways: given an equation like 6 × 4 = 24, write a 'times as many' sentence; given a sentence, write the equation.
For 35 = 5 × 7, write both multiplicative comparisons it supports: '35 is 5 times as many as 7' and '35 is 7 times as many as 5'.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Times as many' describes a multiplicative relationship (larger = n × smaller) and 'more than' describes an additive relationship (larger = smaller + n); the operation you actually carry out depends on which quantity is unknown (e.g. finding the smaller quantity from 'Sam has 3 times as many as Jo, and Sam has 24' means dividing). Translation must run reliably in both directions, and one equation can encode two multiplicative comparisons.

activities.title: Talk it through: times, or just more?
feedback: If reasoning drifts to adding, redirect to copies: how many copies of the smaller quantity make the larger one?
Accept an answer only when it names the relationship (copies-of / groups), not just a number.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue may build the distinction and translation habit through explanation (efficacy untested); the scaling relationship itself is most vivid in built or drawn bars, so use discussion to accompany, not replace, the modelling.
sourceClaims: Comparison bar models support multiplicative comparison; multiplicative and additive comparison must be explicitly contrasted.
learnerActions: With a character comparing two collections, answer the recurring question: 'Does "times as many" mean add, or multiply? How do you know?'
Justify each answer by describing the bars or copies you would draw, e.g. '3 times as many is 3 copies, so multiply'.
When the character offers an additive answer to a 'times as many' problem, explain why that is wrong and give the correct multiplicative reading.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why 'times as many' is multiplicative, and defending it against an additive suggestion, strengthens the distinction and the translation habit.

constraints: Tier A (age 9): translate '4 times as many' to ×4 and draw the two bars. Tier B (age 9–10): write an equation for a verbal multiplicative-comparison statement. Tier C (age 10): distinguish multiplicative from additive comparison and explain both comparisons a single equation encodes.

This is a NEW meaning of multiplication beyond equal groups: a relationship between two quantities where one is 'n times' the other. Keep the relational meaning central; do not let it collapse back into plain equal-groups counting.
Always contrast multiplicative and additive comparisons using the SAME numbers so the difference is visible, since children conflate them.

Move translation both ways (verbal→equation and equation→verbal); the standard requires both interpreting equations as comparisons and representing verbal statements as equations, so do not drill only one direction.
Sorting/matching tasks can check recognition and translation; they do not themselves build the scaling intuition, so pair them with bar-building or tower-building activities.

Paper or cube bars have slight real thickness and are approximations of the idealised bar diagram, and an on-screen scalable bar is also a model; what carries the comparison is the bar LENGTH, not the material. Both media are fine; neither is uniquely necessary.
A dynamic scaling dial, live recolouring, or an additive 'ghost' bar are optional aids that may make the contrast vivid; static drawn or stacked bars can achieve the same insight.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic check (all correct as used): red=7, ×5 → 35 while 7+5=12; 4 cubes × 4 = 16 while 4+4=8; 3×8=24; red=5, ×4 → 20; 6×4=24. The original source's additive 'ghost' example for red=7 used '12' in one place and '7+3=10' in another; the ×5 case gives 7+5=12. Learner text uses 12 consistently for the +5 additive comparison; the stray '7+3=10' appears to be a leftover ×3 example and was not carried forward.
Two source claims (CCSS-M 4.OA.1 and NCETM guidance) were marked verified:false in the original; their cited principles are retained but their verification status is unconfirmed here.

The bar re-reading '7 is one-fifth of 35' introduces division/fraction language and is the reciprocal of the bar's multiplicative comparison, not one of the standard's two 'n times as many' comparisons (those — '35 is 5 times 7' and '35 is 7 times 5' — are written in the sort-and-translate activity, where both factors appear). It is included as scoped enrichment and may be simplified to '7 is one of the five equal copies' for Tier A/B learners.

Independent re-audit confirms: no learner question offers an additive reading as a valid/correct option; the additive value (8, or +5 → 12) appears only as a contrasted wrong reading that is explicitly corrected; the two distinct insights (reciprocal reading of bars vs two multiplicative comparisons of the equation) are kept in separate activities and do not contradict each other.

probeDeeper: You said 16. What does '4 times as tall' tell you about how many red towers fit into blue?
If blue were '4 MORE than red' instead, how tall would it be? How is that different from '4 times'?
The red tower is 4 and blue is 16. How many times as tall is blue — and how do you know?
What if red had been 5 cubes and blue was 4 times as tall — how tall is blue?
assess.correctAnswer: 16 cubes. A child reasoning correctly interprets '4 times as tall' multiplicatively: the blue tower is four copies of the red tower's height, 4 × 4 = 16 — not 4 more than red. The explanation names that 'times as many' compares by how many COPIES/groups, not by how many more.

errorPatterns.pattern: reads 'N times as many/tall' additively — interprets '4 times as tall as 4' as '4 more', giving 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: build it: stack four separate red towers end to end to SEE four copies; contrast with '4 more' by adding just 4 cubes, so 'times as many' and 'more than' become physically different.
errorPatterns.distractor: 8 cubes (4 times as tall means 4 taller, so 4 + 4)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child answers 8 and explains 'it's 4 taller' or 'add 4'

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses which quantity is the referent — makes red the multiple of blue, or divides when they should multiply
errorPatterns.nextMove: name the '1 unit' explicitly (red = one unit of height) and show blue is 4 of those units; use a double-number-line with red at 1 and blue at 4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child sets up 4 ÷ 4 or treats blue as the unit being copied

errorPatterns.pattern: gets 16 by rote multiplication but cannot say it means 'four copies of red' — no comparative meaning attached
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach multiplication; ask 'how many red towers would you need to match blue?' to surface the comparison already implicit in their answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child computes 4×4 correctly yet, asked what '4 times as tall' means, restates the calculation rather than the copies-of relationship

responseLevels.gap: answers 8 (additive) or divides; interprets 'times as many' as 'more than'.
responseLevels.full: gives 16, explains '4 times as tall' as four copies of the red unit, distinguishes it from '4 more', and can find the multiplier when given both quantities.
responseLevels.partial: computes 16 correctly but explains it only as a calculation, not as 'four copies of red' — cannot cleanly contrast multiplicative with additive comparison when probed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The red tower is 4 cubes tall. The blue tower is 4 TIMES as tall as the red one. How tall is the blue tower — and explain what '4 times as tall' means about how the two towers compare.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The signature error is reading multiplicative comparison as additive ('4 times as tall' → 4 + 4 = 8, 'four taller'). Asking for the meaning, not just the number, forces the child to reveal whether they see copies-of vs more-than. A child who answers 16 but explains it as 'add 4 four times to 4' also reveals a shaky grasp on probing.
